read.bigIdea: By the time you can taste it, it’s late.
read.where: A trained taster can catch an infected line, and the pre-shift check (Level 3) tastes every tap. But the Draught Beer Quality Manual warns that bacteria start growing **long before** anyone can taste them, so maintenance has to be **preventive**. Tests help: **ATP** swabs (a luminometer reading of rinse water) and **color-indicator** cleaners show how clean a line is, but can’t tell beer-spoilers from harmless yeast. **Plating** samples and growing them is the only way to **identify** the organism; it’s slow and costly, so it’s for a line that keeps going bad.

stops.text: **What** is growing, for a problem line.

read.mixup: A line that tastes fine today isn’t proof it’s clean. Infections show up in taste last.

sections.name: What grows in a dirty line

read.where: Within days of a new system going in, **biofilm** starts building on everything beer touches. The manual’s table of draft faults: **diacetyl** (butter, butterscotch, a slick feel) is the **most common** off-flavor from dirty draft systems, most likely from **Pediococcus**; **lactic** sourness (sour milk) from **Lactobacillus**, though it takes a big infection to taste; **acetic** (vinegar) from **Acetobacter**, which starts in dirty **drains, spill trays, bar tops and rags** and spreads to the faucets, often because faucets weren’t taken apart every two weeks. Once a line is infected it’s hard, sometimes impossible, to clean: replace infected parts and lines, **replace any keg tapped into it**, and alternate caustic and acid cleans.
read.mixup: Not every diacetyl is the line. A little is allowed in some English and Czech beers; check the same beer from a fresh package before you blame the system.

read.where: When a draft tastes wrong, find where the fault lives. Taste the **same beer** from a can, bottle or a fresh keg. If the package is fine, the problem is on **our side**: one bad line points to its **faucet, coupler or keg**; several lines with the same butter or vinegar note point to the **cleaning** or the whole system. If the package tastes the same, it’s the **beer**: age (past its date), **heat** (the manual says keep draft below **50°F**, and above **80°F** for any time it’s likely ruined), or the brewery. Then **pull it**, note the **date code** and keg, and call the distributor.

stops.name: Act
stops.text: Pull it, note the **date code**, call.

read.mixup: Changing the keg doesn’t fix an infected line. A fresh keg on a dirty line goes bad too.

video.title: Clean glass? What your beer foam is telling you | The Curiosity Desk

read.bigIdea: A dirty glass ruins a clean line.
read.where: Some faults never touch the line. A **beer-clean** glass has no film, foam-killing residue or **sanitizer** smell. In a three-tub sink, the manual says: **detergent** that isn’t fat- or oil-based, a running **cold rinse**, then sanitizer at the right strength (chlorine **100 ppm**, quats **200 ppm**, unless local rules differ): more isn’t better. **Air-dry** glasses on a wire rack; towels leave lint and odors, rubber mats and smooth surfaces trap smells. Keep the bar glass machine for **glasses only**, never food or dairy. Chill glasses at **36–40°F**, never frozen: ice in the glass makes foam.
read.mixup: Bubbles clinging to the side of the glass aren’t carbonation. They mean the glass isn’t beer-clean.
